To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the coronary microcirculatory response to exercise in the failing human heart is blunted and that this is due, at least in part, to endothelial dysfunction.

the myocardial microcirculation is a key regulator of myocardial oxygen balance and that the coronary microcirculatory response to exercise is altered in heart failure and may be improved by exercise training.
the heart's response during exercise can provide insight into the pathophysiology of heart failure and that exercise training can improve coronary microvascular dysfunction and oxidative stress.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the coronary microcirculatory function in exercise-induced cardiac dysfunction.
the role of the coronary microcirculatory endothelium as a mediator of myocardial oxygen balance during exercise.
understanding the mechanisms of exercise-induced changes in myocardial oxygen demand and supply and their implications for coronary microvascular function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the beneficial effects of acute exercise are due to increased coronary microvascular blood flow.
coronary microvascular dysfunction is a key player in the pathophysiology of heart failure and that exercise training is an important tool to improve myocardial oxygen balance and cardiac function.
exercise training improves myocardial oxygen balance and cardiac function in the failing heart, and that this effect is at least in part mediated through the coronary microcirculatory system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the coronary microcirculatory dysfunction in heart failure is a major contributor to the development of heart failure and that exercise training is an effective therapeutic tool to improve coronary microvascular function in patients with heart failure.
exercise training can improve the myocardial oxygen supply-demand balance, which is of great interest for patients with heart failure.
coronary microvascular dysfunction in the heart is a common feature of heart failure and exercise training may be a useful strategy to restore myocardial oxygen balance.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the coronary microvascular endothelial dysfunction that develops in heart failure and in the metabolic syndrome is not only a marker of the disease state, but it is also a major contributor to disease progression.
the coronary microvascualture is not only a conduit for oxygen delivery, but also an important player in the regulation of myocardial oxygen balance and cardiac function.
exercise training may be a powerful intervention to improve coronary microvascular function and, thus, myocardial oxygen balance in the failing heart.
